evidence.notes: `build_nat_prelude` admits this theorem through the trusted `Kernel::add_declaration` gate, which re-checks the proof term against the stated type, so producing this row at all is a machine-checked proof. The statement is universally quantified over BOTH the combinator `f : Bool -> Bool -> Bool` and `n : Nat`, and holds unconditionally -- no hypothesis on `f` (in particular, no `f false false = false`) is needed, because fuel is `m = 0` at this call, so the outer `Nat.rec` hits `bitwiseAux`'s fuel-exhaustion row directly and that row IS this statement's RHS by construction: the proof is `Eq.refl`. `nat_theorem_inventory` exits non-zero for a name that does not exist, and `grep -Ec` consumes the pipe and the count is tested, so the exit status depends on what the run found. Anchored with `^Nat\.bitwise_zero_left[[:space:]]` (verified exactly 1 row).
evidence.supports: forall f n, bitwise f 0 n = if f false true then n else 0

evidence.notes: Instantiates the universal theorem at two concrete `f` witnesses built inline (`and_fn`, `or_fn` -- this prelude declares no top-level `Bool.and`/`Bool.or`) and a concrete `n = 7`, confirming the ADMITTED TYPE at each instantiation `def_eq`s the expected specialization: at `and_fn` (absorbing on this side) `bitwise and_fn 0 7` reduces to `0`, at `or_fn` (identity on this side) it reduces to `7` -- with negative controls asserting each instantiation does NOT also state the other's value, so a definition that ignored `f` entirely (always returning `n`, or always `0`) cannot pass both.
evidence.supports: the theorem specializes correctly at both an absorbing and a non-absorbing f

evidence.notes: `nat_axiom_inventory --require-axiom-free nat` enumerates the built Nat environment and exits non-zero unless it admits no Axiom, Opaque or Quotient declaration. `Nat.bitwiseAux` uses the same structural fuel device as `Nat.landAux`/`Nat.lorAux`/`Nat.ldiffAux` rather than Mathlib's well-founded `Nat.bitwise`, so nothing here needs `WellFounded`/`Quot.sound`/`propext`; this command is what makes the axiom-freedom claim falsifiable rather than asserted. Measured with `Nat.bitwise` landed: `nat: axiom=0 opaque=0 quotient=0 total_trusted=0`.

formal.statement: ((x0 : ((x0 : Bool) -> ((x1 : Bool) -> Bool))) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> Eq.{1} AxNat (AxNat.bitwise x0 AxNat.zero x1) (Bool.rec.{1} (fun (x2 : Bool) => AxNat) AxNat.zero x1 (x0 Bool.false Bool.true))))

notes:
formal.statement is `Kernel::render_lean` of the admitted type, taken verbatim from `nat_theorem_inventory`, not transcribed by hand. `AxNat` is the kernel's CONSTRUCTED inductive `Nat` (the `Ax` is *axeyum*, not *axiomatized*) -- the `nat` prelude's trusted surface measures zero.

`Nat.bitwise` is the GENERAL `f : Bool -> Bool -> Bool` combinator two earlier lanes declined to build, citing `f` threaded through mismatched-length base cases as more construction than one lane's scope. Landed here now that `Nat.land`/`Nat.lor`/`Nat.ldiff` (each a specialization Mathlib routes through `Nat.bitwise`, landed directly instead) established the fuel-recursion device and, critically, the absorbing-zero-vs-not distinction the general base case has to make PER `f` rather than at compile time. That distinction is resolved by evaluating `f` at the two boundary Bool literals (`f false true` for the `m = 0` row, `f true false` for the `n = 0` row) and gating with `bool_select_nat`, identical in shape to the zero-guards `land`/`lor`/`ldiff` already build -- no new combinator, no new primitive, no new height dependency beyond one extra bound `f` threaded through every closure. See `crates/axeyum-lean-kernel/src/nat_prelude/bitwise.rs`'s module doc for the full derivation, including what was NOT attempted (a universal `forall m n, bitwise and m n = land m n` equivalence proof, sized past this lane's scope; `F:nat-bitwise-and-eq-land-three-five` and its `lor`/`xor` siblings are the strongest available check without it).

Does not flip any `F:ml430-nat-bitwise-*` fact -- those are a separate, held-out mirror population and untouched by this lane.

statement: For every bit-combining function f and every natural n, the general bitwise combinator applied to (f, 0, n) equals n when f false true holds and 0 otherwise.
title: bitwise f 0 n = if f false true then n else 0
